title: CJP: India 'cockroach' leaders detained after entering barricaded protest site
description: Leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were detained early on Tuesday after they entered a heavily-guarded protest site and chanted slogans de
body: Leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were detained early on Tuesday after they entered a heavily-guarded protest site and chanted slogans demanding the country's election chief resign over a controversial revision of electoral rolls.Party founder Abhijeet Dipke shared a video showing Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das being taken away by police from Jantar Mantar, a historic Delhi observatory popular for protests.Footage showed the two - along with others - climbing over police barricades before chanting slogans while holding the Indian flag.Prime Minister Narendra Modi's opponents allege the voter list revision benefits his party, a charge it and the Election Commission reject.There have been days of protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.Police have stepped up security across Delhi as demonstrators challenge restrictions on where protests can be held. Early on Tuesday, Dipke, Das and Ranka all shared videos showing Das and Ranka entering Jantar Mantar."You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X. Das also posted a message declaring that the site had been "reclaimed" and that they were being detained.It was not immediately clear where police had taken the leaders.Ranka later appeared on an Instagram live broadcast from a police bus alongside other detainees where they appeared cheerful and said they would not back down.The detentions came a day after the federal home ministry announced that Jantar Mantar, long associated with public protests in Delhi, would no longer be a designated protest venue. Authorities instead identified three alternative locations where demonstrations can be held with permission.Before the decision, the CJP had met Delhi Police officials to seek permission for a peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar and had warned that it would announce further demonstrations if it received no response."30 mins after we went to Delhi Police asking for a date when we can go to Jantar Mantar, Jantar Mantar was de-notified as a protest site," Ranka had earlier posted on X.Most of the party's leadership has been in Delhi in recent days. Dipke, however, had travelled to his hometown in Maharashtra after the death of his grandmother. He was among several CJP leaders detained ahead of a planned demonstration on Saturday and was released the next day.The CJP had called for a protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday, but authorities imposed extensive security restrictions across the capital to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site.Several metro stations were closed, train services were disrupted and thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed.Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.Separately, opposition parties held a march in Delhi on Monday from Connaught Place - a major shopping district in the heart of the capital - to the Supreme Court.The Congress, India's main opposition party, also petitioned the Supreme Court on Monday, challenging the Election Commission's voter revision exercise, which has resulted in tens of millions of names being removed from electoral rolls.Critics say the exercise risks excluding eligible voters and making it harder for them to prove their eligibility. Anger over the revision exercise intensified after The Indian Express reported that Kumar had disregarded concerns raised by the two other election commissioners over changes to voter registration. The Election Commission has said its decisions were unanimous.The current protests follow student-led demonstrations earlier this year over exam irregularities and demands for education reforms. The CJP led weeks of action that culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.The group began as online satire after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May. He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people seeking change.After the summer protests, the CJP evolved into a pressure group, tapping into wider anger over unemployment, exam irregularities and government accountability.

schema.headline: CJP: India 'cockroach' leaders detained after entering barricaded protest site

title: Horrified witnesses recount fatal rollercoaster incident at Six Flags
description: Warning: This article contains some graphic detailsOne person has died and others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at an amusement pa
body: Warning: This article contains some graphic detailsOne person has died and others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the US state of Georgia.The Cobb County Police Department is investigating the fatality at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24km) from Atlanta, a local official confirmed. The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, with riders being helped off by workers.Horrified witnesses have told local media they saw a man ejected from the ride - something the BBC has not verified. Six Flags said it was temporarily closing nine rides across the US and Canada as a precaution.It said it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones".Lisa Cupid, the chairwoman of Cobb County's governing body, said police detectives with the local major crimes unit "are investigating the circumstances surrounding this incident". Officials have not said how the person died, or how the other riders were injured. The BBC has contacted local police and fire authorities, as well as park officials. The identity of the person who died has also not been disclosed.Local outlet 11 Alive quoted a witness saying the man had come loose from his seat and had then struck the rollercoaster and some of his fellow riders before falling onto the roof of a nearby haunted house attraction.The incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion, the witness added.A husband and wife, who were on the ride, also told 11 Alive that the man fell from the ride and was struck by it. They said workers at the park had checked their safety harnesses before the ride set off.  "We were having a great time and to just screaming 'Oh my God, what is happening?'," the woman said.Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she was in line to ride Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a girl covered in blood.Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off".Brittany Landry, who believes she saw the man ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears."I broke because we were just on there," Landry said.A park spokesperson said in a statement that its team and local authorities had responded immediately and that they were co-operating on an investigation into the incident.Mableton Mayor Michael Owens said the city's public safety director was co-ordinating with local police and park security on the situation.The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.Six Flags is the largest amusement park operator in North America, with 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.The death in Georgia comes just weeks after one of Six Flags' parks in southern California announced it would close the popular X2 roller coaster after more than 100 people alleged brain injuries from the ride.Six Flags said that ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire the attraction because it was "the right thing to do".Were you at Six Flags? Did you witness what happened? Get in touch here

schema.headline: Horrified witnesses recount fatal rollercoaster incident at Six Flags

title: Immigration agents search congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
description: US immigration agents have searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar as part of a criminal investigation.Homeland Security Investigatio
body: US immigration agents have searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar as part of a criminal investigation.Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents "executed a judicially authorised search warrant" for the property in the Washington DC area, a US justice department spokesperson said. The search "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation", the spokesperson said, but no further details were given. The US Congress is currently out of session and it is unclear if Omar was at the home.Omar, a Democrat and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, described the search on social media as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement"."For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said in the post. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said he had "nothing to do" with the justice department's investigation into Omar, while describing her as a "complainer" and a "terrible person".The Republican president said of the Somali-born congresswoman: "She comes from a country that is a non-country. "And then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution."At a rally in Ohio later on Monday, Trump referred to the search of Omar's home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."Trump went on to denigrate Somalis in the US more generally, which was greeted with chants of "deport" in the crowd, US media reported.Omar's communications director, Jacklyn Rogers, called Monday morning's raid "an outrageous abuse of power" by the Trump administration, and said the congresswoman "has done nothing wrong".The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear. An ally of Omar gave an update to the BBC World Service's Newsday programme. Asma Mohammed said: "She is doing well, she's let everyone know that she's okay and that she is used to attacks from the president but this is a new low from him."During Monday's search, a BBC crew saw several agents at Omar's home, some carrying boxes to a van. News of the search was first reported by Fox News, which said the investigation was about immigration paperwork filed by her late father when Omar was a child.The timing of the raid - 22 days before the November midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in Congress for the next two years - raised concerns from Omar's fellow Democrats.The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it is being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or to disadvantage a candidate.Leading Democrats in the House of Representatives said in a statement that Omar had long been targeted with "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations" by Trump. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," they said.Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans and earlier this year, a fellow congresswoman, Nancy Mace of South Carolina, unsuccessfully sought a subpoena for her records.Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", and made allegations of marital fraud against Omar. Separately, the White House's border tsar, Tom Homan, told Fox News that Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.Omar denied these allegations last month. "I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said in a campaign fundraising email. Trump has previously suggested that Omar "should go back" to Somalia and that she should be deported. US citizenship is required to serve as a member of the House.Omar has responded to Trump's insults and attacks, describing them as an "unhealthy and creepy obsession".The president has also singled out the Somali-American community. Last week, he wrote on social media that Minnesota "is being taken over by Somali immigrants" and "the people of Minnesota must fight back".Some Republicans celebrated Monday's search. "Nobody is above the law," said Tom Emmer, who also represents Minnesota in the House. "We look forward to learning more details about this raid and investigation. ACCOUNTABILITY IS COMING!"Omar is the first Somali American elected to the House and she represents a district in the Minneapolis area. She and Michigan Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women elected to Congress.Omar won re-election two years ago with 74% of the vote. Senior political leaders in Minnesota have criticised the search. Governor Tim Walz, a fellow Democrat, said: "Americans see this for what it is - President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election."Minnesota Senator Tina Smith called it "a transparent attempt to interfere in our elections".Additional reporting by Ione Wells

schema.headline: Immigration agents search congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home

title: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
description: Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia att
body: Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities.""I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added.Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday.On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said.Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire".On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district.Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured.When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire".Asked about the ceasefire on Monday, Trump said they agreed "because I said you agree", adding that the war "has to get settled". "That war is a disaster if you see the numbers," he said. For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure, disrupting energy supplies on both sides.Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter.In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025.Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year.

schema.headline: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says

title: Joseph Kabila: DR Congo ex-president named leader of new M23 rebel coalition
description: Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila has been named the leader of a new rebel coalition seeking to oust the government.The Front for the Refoundat
body: Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila has been named the leader of a new rebel coalition seeking to oust the government.The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it aimed to coordinate "resistance forces" to end "tyranny" in Democratic Republic of Congo and would pursue the goal "by all means, including force".Its unveiling on Monday is the clearest indication so far of Kabila's direct involvement in an armed movement a year after he was sentenced to death in absentia for treason. He had previously denied having links to the M23 rebel group.The Congolese government has not commented.Claude Ibalanky, the coalition's adviser, announced the group's leadership at a press conference at Kabila's residence in Goma, the largest city in eastern DR Congo, which has been under the control of the M23 since last year. Video released by the group showed Kabila signing documents at the group's declaration along with other leaders.M23 leader Sultani Makenga will serve as one of Kabila's four deputies in the new movement. The other three also come from the AFC-M23 alliance which last year seized much of mineral-rich eastern DR Congo.The announcement of the new group comes days after Kabila delivered an address in which he said he would set out how Congolese people should act to "rescue" their country.On Friday, Kabila accused President Félix Tshisekedi's government of disregarding proposals he had put forward last year, including some aimed at ending the conflict in eastern DR Congo.Kabila also accused the government of undermining constitutional rule, mismanaging the economy and failing to improve security. He further alleged arbitrary arrests of political opponents and military officers.The government has not publicly responded to those claims.Kabila, 55, ruled DR Congo from 2001 until January 2019, when Tshisekedi took office following a disputed election.The two were once political allies, forming an informal power-sharing arrangement after the transfer of power. They later fell out and Kabila went into self-imposed exile in 2023 before returning to Goma last year.Tshisekedi's second term ends in 2028 but in May he said that elections, which are due then, may not be held because of the conflict.He also hinted that he may seek re-election for a third term "if the people want". The parliament has since passed a bill that could pave the way for a referendum that could remove the constitution's two-term limit.Last month, authorities clashed with protesters holding demonstrations in the capital against the proposed changes.Richard Moncrieff, who monitors Africa's Great Lakes region for the International Crisis Group (ICG) says the new coalition is aimed at trying to enlarge the rebellion.He argues that through his "higher profile", Kabila hopes to get support from people dissatisfied with Tshisekedi "beyond the very narrow political base that the M23 enjoys". The analyst says this appears to be Kabila's objective, to draw more senior Congolese army officers to his side and "lessen the reliance of the M23 on its Rwandan backers".Kabila came to power after the assassination of his father Laurent Kabila, who headed a national rebellion in the 1990s, backed by Rwanda. His forces marched across the country, starting in the east, before taking over in the capital Kinshasa, some 1,500km (1,000 miles) away. Moncrieff  says Kabila is drawing on that past to proclaim the illegitimacy of Tshisekedi's government. He however says it won't be easy to seize power like his father, partly because the US has imposed sanctions on Kabila, which he says presumes American support for DR Congo's government.In May the US imposed sweeping sanctions on Kabila, accusing him of backing the M23, providing financial support, encouraging defections from the Congolese army. Kabila said the measures were unjustified and politically motivated.The US said they were part of a wider effort to support last year's peace deal between DR Congo and Rwanda that it brokered.The latest events show peace negotiations are "going nowhere and attempting to gain control on the ground is the priority for all parties," the ICG analyst says.

schema.headline: Joseph Kabila: DR Congo ex-president named leader of new M23 rebel coalition

title: Bulgarian PM summons Russian ambassador after ship sinks in Black Sea drone attack
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, One of the struck ships has been identified as the Maltese-flagged Chelsea-3, registered in UkraineByJaroslav Luki
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, One of the struck ships has been identified as the Maltese-flagged Chelsea-3, registered in UkraineByJaroslav LukivUpdated 35 minutes agoBulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has summoned the Russian ambassador after two merchant ships were struck by drones off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast and one of them sank.Six crew members on the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity were rescued and 10 others are missing, according to Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov, after it went down 17 nautical miles (31km) east of the village of Krapets having sent a distress signal.The other ship, the Ukrainian owned Chelsea-3, was hit by drones 18 nautical miles from the town of Byala and all 15 crew were rescued.The attacks come a week after two other commercial ships were hit by sea and aerial drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. One of the ships, the Alfa Watan, sank and all 10 crew, including nine Syrians, are presumed dead.Radev convened an emergency meeting on Tuesday and said he had summoned Russian envoy Eleonora Mitrofanova. Although there was no conclusive evidence of blame on "either side... the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation", he said.Mitrofanova was later quoted by Bulgarian media as telling Radev she had no information from Russia's defence ministry relating to the latest attacks. She also said these strikes could have been a provocation by a third party. Image source, ReutersImage caption, Five crew members of Chelsea-3 suffered minor injuries in Tuesday's attacksBulgaria is a Nato member, and Radev also spoke to secretary general Mark Rutte about the latest attacks."Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea," Rutte said after the talks. "We have already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank and will continue to monitor the security environment, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed," he added.The Dignity and Chelsea-3 were struck just outside Bulgarian territorial waters, in its Black Sea "exclusive economic zone".If this had happened just a few nautical miles to the west, Article 5 of the Nato treaty could have been triggered. The article defines an armed attack on one member of the military alliance as an attack on all."Escalation in the Black Sea is steadily increasing," Bulgaria's defence minister later told reporters after speaking to his counterparts in Romania and Turkey. "We see this conflict drawing ever closer to our territorial waters.""We assume the drones are Russian," he said, as it would have been "illogical" for Ukraine to target its own ships.Rumen Radev had earlier asked Nato and the EU for technical assistance in investigating the previous attacks that took place on 6 October, indicating it was unclear who was behind them.Radev came to office during the summer and although he has rejected suggestions that he is "pro-Russian", his government has until now avoided blaming Moscow.Ukraine has directly accused Russia of staging the latest attacks and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke on Tuesday of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable".Russia's military has not publicly commented on the issue. It has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the Black Sea, particularly the western side, as part of its war against Ukraine. The same day that two ships were targeted off Bulgaria last week, Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi.Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports - and cited attacks in the ports of Mykolaiv and Chornomorsk last week, along with one in the Black Sea. However, Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Rumen Radev (middle right) said the attack was "absolutely unacceptable" before meeting Russia's ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova (middle left)Meeting his security chiefs on Tuesday, Bulgaria's prime minister said: "Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable".While the search continued for the rest of the crew from the HS Dignity, Radev said five crew members on board the Chelsea-3 were being treated for minor injuries. The cargo ship is registered in the southern Ukraine port of Odesa.Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said "Russia's latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's territorial waters... once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea"."The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage. This must be met with strength," he added.Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea.Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

schema.headline: Bulgarian PM summons Russian ambassador after ship sinks in Black Sea drone attack

title: RJ Mitte: Breaking Bad actor dies aged 34
description: Mitte, who grew up in Louisiana, was a young teen when he auditioned for the breakthrough role after moving to Los Angeles to support his younger sist
body: Mitte, who grew up in Louisiana, was a young teen when he auditioned for the breakthrough role after moving to Los Angeles to support his younger sister's acting career in 2005.He had said that his first audition in Los Angeles was for a California state public service announcement for an anti-meth commercial. "Fast forward to auditioning for Breaking Bad, which is still, in my opinion, an anti-meth thing because it doesn't end well for anyone," he said on the Joe Vulpis Podcast earlier this month.His character was based on the show's creator Vince Gilligan's late friend who had a more severe case of cerebral palsy and used forearm crutches, which Mitte did not require. Mitte was seen as playing the role with honesty and accessibility, cracking jokes as a teen whose health condition was rarely mentioned in the series.Breaking Bad aired on US cable broadcaster AMC for five seasons from 2008-13. After shooting to fame, Mitte fought for more varied roles and complex depictions of characters with disabilities, both visible and invisible."Whenever awards season rolls around, we always hope to see a diverse group of projects that reflect all of us, in body and mind," he told the BBC in 2021. "Watching the awareness grow around disability representation has been great to see, but breakthroughs sometimes come in pieces and moments instead of larger change," he said.Mitte's other on-screen credits include Hannah Montana, Switched at Birth, Westhampton and his latest project, Talking to Strangers, which came out earlier this year. Additional reporting by Rebecka Pieder.If you have been affected by the issues raised in this story help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: RJ Mitte: Breaking Bad actor dies aged 34

title: Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC
description: Ukraine has stabilised the front line and "broken Russia's ability to advance" by killing so many of its men, Ukraine's former commander-in-chief has
body: Ukraine has stabilised the front line and "broken Russia's ability to advance" by killing so many of its men, Ukraine's former commander-in-chief has said in an interview with the BBC.Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi made the comments in an exclusive interview, his first since he was dramatically forced from his post in the summer.He addressed his sacking, disagreeing with his critics who declared him too "old school" to command Ukraine's new, technologically advanced forces.He also pushed back against allegations made by soldiers who previously served under him, who told the BBC they were ordered to remain at their positions even when they were almost surrounded by Russians, leading to high losses.Syrskyi said that Moscow's overall losses in the war were six times higher than Ukraine's. "If you count only dead, then it's up to 11 times," he added.Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially release the numbers of their dead. Ukraine's military says it inflicted record losses this year on Russian soldiers in September, although that cannot be verified.UK intelligence chiefs estimate Russia has lost around half a million men killed in Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022. The US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies meanwhile believes, external Ukraine has lost up to 150,000 troops killed by June 2026.He says this difference in death toll – as well as technological advances, and a strategy of attacking weak points in Russia's lines while containing their advances in other parts – accounts for the current stalemate at the front.In the first six months of 2026, Russia managed overall to seize 61 sq km, the general said. "It's an indication that the front line has been stabilised."The Institute for Study of War (ISW) has also confirmed this trend. One of its recent reports, external says that in September 2026, Moscow lost more territory than it took.Syrskyi was appointed Ukraine's commander-in-chief in 2024. He had previously won praise for defending Kyiv at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, and for leading the successful counteroffensive east of Kharkiv in the autumn of that year.But President Volodymyr Zelensky fired Syrskyi this summer, amid a major disagreement with then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.Fedorov had said that instead of adapting to the realities of the changing war, the army under Syrskyi had blocked his initiatives.Zelensky initially fired Fedorov, as tensions burst into the open between the two men. But mass street protests then forced the president to also fire Syrskyi, replacing him with Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43.Syrskyi told the BBC that he had "disagreements" with Fedorov because the latter "didn't take into consideration the interests of the army" when procuring weapons and supplies.Fedorov had created an "imbalance" in supplies, Syrskyi said. He had prioritised drones while overlooking key front-line kit such as unmanned ground vehicles, pick-up trucks and motorbikes. Even with drones, Syrskyi said, there were shortages as the army got only half of what they needed.Fedorov was a popular young minister who was known for his digital and technological initiatives. Many contrasted him with Syrskyi, who critics thought was not fit to lead the new technological arms race with Russia.But Syrskyi disagrees with such criticism. It was during his time the use of drones reached this new, unprecedented level, including deep strikes more than 2,000km (1,200 miles) behind enemy lines, he said. Ukraine was the first country to create the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch of armed forces, under his command: now, he said, drones account for 80% of Russia's losses.Under his military leadership, however, Ukrainian troops undertook chaotic withdrawals from the eastern cities of Avdiivka and Vuhledar, and from around Pokrovsk. Soldiers who spoke to the BBC in the past complained that they were ordered to remain at their positions at any costs. By the time they were told to pull back, it was often too late as they were almost surrounded by Russian troops.Syrskyi does not deny that such situations occur on the front line. But he told the BBC that Ukraine was fighting against a far more powerful army. In 2025, the ratio of jets and bombs was 18 to one in Moscow's favour, he said. In the same year, Russia had two-and-a-half times more artillery pieces and shells than Ukraine. And with four million militarily trained men who they can mobilise, Russian forces can create chances to push through, he argued.One of Syrskyi's most famous operations was an incursion into Russia's Kursk region that started in August 2024. It ended with a dramatic retreat the following spring, which some soldiers described as "catastrophic". Syrskyi, however, insisted that the Kursk operation was "a necessity"."In the summer 2024, Russian forces were pushing along all main directions on the front line with up to six times more troops than we had," he explained.The Kursk incursion disrupted Russia's offensive and forced Moscow to redirect troops, giving Ukraine a respite and a chance for its stretched brigades in the east and south to recover, Syrskyi said.He also had strong words for European allies who doubt that Russia may have territorial ambitions beyond Ukraine. He advised European partners to start preparing for the war now and "drop all illusions that [it] will not come".He also said he believed Ukraine's war was going to become even more technological. There will be more robots, automated systems and artificial intelligence (AI). "Even ordinary weapons now get an AI-based control system to enhance their capabilities," he said.Such technologies can give a new life to conventional weapons like tanks. Both Russia and Ukraine were now racing to develop "active systems of defence" to protect armoured vehicles, Syrskyi said.But he insisted that "the human role will remain definitive [on the battlefield] because [people] will need to control those systems".

schema.headline: Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC

title: Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to evade tax on Abramovich’s wealth, BBC finds
description: The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.Accounts s
body: The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism. For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history.Abramovich's close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggestAn email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read.MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money.A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree". MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI.This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus.Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets.So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax.Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said.Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law."In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus.MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune.It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public.Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier.MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000.Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear.

schema.headline: Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to evade tax on Abramovich’s wealth, BBC finds

title: Where the US midterm elections will be won and lost
description: ByMike HillsVisual Journalism teamAmericans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out.Thousand
body: ByMike HillsVisual Journalism teamAmericans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out.Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress.Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome.Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent.Midterms come at bad time for TrumpOne of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform.He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s.It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%.Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate.But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years.The battle for the HouseThe current Republican majority in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, is as thin as it gets - they have 218 representatives, which is the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them.Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November.But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner.The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party.Of those 21 toss-ups, 15 are currently held by Republicans and six by Democrats. If the Democrats win five of those on top of 28 districts classed as likely or leaning Democratic, they will win the House.Historically, the midterms see a high number of seats changing hands in the House, usually in a protest against the White House. The average number lost by the president's party is 27, according to data, external going back to 1934. Of those 23 elections, the president's party has only made gains in three.The battle for the SenateThe Republicans have a slightly stronger hold on the Senate. They hold 53 of the 100 seats while the Democrats have 45 and two independents who also vote with them.Members of the Senate serve six-year terms so roughly a third are up for election every two years.Thirty-five seats are up for grabs in November but analysis by the Cook Political Report suggests that only seven of them are toss-ups that could go either way.Of those toss-ups, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus the four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats.They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.What are the key issues for voters?Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters.The president proudly declared that gas was "now below $2.30 [£1.74] a gallon in most states" in his State of the Union address on 24 February. But the war with Iran began four days later, disrupting Middle Eastern energy supplies and causing gas to hit $4 (£3.03) in the US.The war became increasingly unpopular as its consequences reverberated around the world and ultimately hit American consumers in the pocket. One poll carried out in August found 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the situation.Other issues that voters say are important to them include healthcare and immigration.Trump has recently touted his policies around immigration as a big success, citing significantly lower border-crossing figures than in recent years.Many Democratic candidates are focusing on the high costs of US health insurance and the impact of Trump's legislation on access to the healthcare system.Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?Can Trump defy political gravity?Most signs point towards a successful midterms for the Democrats, but it wouldn't be the first time that Trump and his party have outperformed polls if they do win more seats than expected.One of the few things in their favour is their huge financial advantage.At the end of August, the Republican National Committee and its allied groups had more than $600m (£455m) cash on hand, while the Democrats had just under $400m (£303m). On top of that, the Republicans also had more than $400m held by Trump's MAGA Inc group, the main fundraising and spending arm of the "Make America Great Again" political movement.The Republicans are using that financial advantage to buy advertising.More than $1bn worth of political ads were broadcast to US voters in September, according to research firm AdImpact, external. Republicans spent $200m more than the Democrats and outspent them in nearly all of the Senate races classed as toss-ups.Trump will be hoping this late messaging blitz can help convince Republicans to get out and vote in November, boosting turnout and limiting the damage done to him and his party.Whatever the result, attention will quickly turn to the next presidential election in 2028. Trump's unpopularity has dominated the midterms, but with him constitutionally unable to run for a third term the focus will shift to what the Democrats stand for, not just what they stand against.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Where the US midterm elections will be won and lost

title: Hungarian parliament scraps Orbán's anti-LGBTQ measures
description: The Hungarian parliament has voted to amend child protection laws, scrapping measures that stigmatise gay and transgender people. LGBTQ and human righ
body: The Hungarian parliament has voted to amend child protection laws, scrapping measures that stigmatise gay and transgender people. LGBTQ and human rights activists warmly welcomed the move, but called for changes to other Orbán-era laws.The 2021 Child Protection Law, passed by the large Fidesz majority of then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, banned the "portrayal or promotion of homosexuality or transgenderism".Since Orbán's April election defeat, the Tisza government of Péter Magyar has been working to dismantle the previous government's legacy. Minutes after Tuesday's vote, Budapest said the EU had agreed to release €4.2bn (£3.5bn) of funds frozen in the last years of the Fidesz government.The European Commission said last month that the Magyar government had addressed a number of "rule of law breaches affecting the EU budget", and urged EU leaders to unlock the funds , externaland readmit Hungary to two key EU programmes - Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe.Hungary's 2021 law had affected a wide range of other laws, including education and the right of assembly. Magyar's Tisza party commands the same two-thirds majority that Orbán's party used to have, and the measures passed on Tuesday were bundled together by the new government in a package of laws designed to unravel the Fidesz legislation."We are very happy that this got adopted," Tamás Dombos of civil rights group the Háttér Society told the BBC. "We've been fighting this so-called child protection law for five years. There have been problems with the bill submitted to parliament, but most of those problems have been fixed."Both the Fidesz and Tisza governments made child protection central to their image. But while Fidesz under Viktor Orbán appealed to the conservative electorate by identifying gay and transgender people as a threat to public morals, Tisza under Prime Minister Péter Magyar is trying to remove or soften legislation, without actually identifying as a liberal-minded government in favour of full equality.In June 2025, the Gay Pride march through Budapest drew an estimated quarter of a million people, despite a promise by then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to his supporters that he would prevent it happening. Police stood aside despite an official ban, and proceedings against the city mayor and others for organising the festival were later dropped. This year's event went ahead without restrictions.The child protection issue turned from being a strong card in Orbán's hand to become his Achilles heel, when the public found out that his government had supported the pardon of the deputy head of a children's home who had been found guilty of covering up the paedophile crimes of his boss.In his own election campaign, Péter Magyar presented his party as a champion of the rights of children in state care, while painstakingly avoiding the issues of gay and transgender rights, for fear of alienating right-wing voters."We are still knocking on a closed door," Dombos told the BBC, "but at least they are listening on the other side." This marked a major improvement on the Orbán years, he said, where his community felt constantly targeted. Other issues he wanted addressed include the full recognition of same-sex marriage, same-sex couples' rights to adopt children, and the restoration of the right of transgender people to change their names in official documents."I'm very cautious," Magyar said in an interview published in Finnish daily Helsingin Sanomat on Saturday. "As prime minister, it's my duty to represent all Hungarians, and we have sensitive issues, such as the situation of sexual minorities." Fidesz and its sister party, the Christian Democrats, voted against the new amendments to the law on Tuesday."There is no place for the promotion of LGBTQ content in schools or the media," the Christian Democrats said in a statement on their website.

schema.headline: Hungarian parliament scraps Orbán's anti-LGBTQ measures

title: Is Zelensky right to say data centre strikes have taken down Russian bots?
description: Claims that Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres reduced Kremlin-linked bot networks have spread widely online, but experts have told BBC Verify
body: Claims that Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres reduced Kremlin-linked bot networks have spread widely online, but experts have told BBC Verify there is no evidence the attacks have significantly reduced them.Viral social media posts have claimed there has been a significant drop in influence operations in recent days, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky suggesting on Monday there was "less hate, less division and fewer provocations" online because of "fewer bots".Russian influence operations, which promote pro-Kremlin narratives and spread disinformation, have been tracked by researchers and journalists including BBC Verify for more than a decade.These campaigns push disinformation on to people's social media feeds on issues like the Ukraine war or post messages in support of Moscow's interests.Ukraine has struck three of Russian tech giant Yandex's five data centres since 8 October in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian internet hubs.The second of these strikes on Thursday caused Yandex, often referred to as Russia's Google, to announce it was struggling to maintain its services.But claims these attacks have affected Russian disinformation operations, including accounts posting supportive messages about groups including the Make American Great Again (MAGA) movement in the US and the far-right AfD party in Germany, appear to have come from a misinterpretation of data produced by tech firm Cloudflare.Some social media users have been sharing charts of Cloudflare data which show bot activity using Yandex's network has declined.While bots are commonly associated with fake social media accounts that may post false, divisive and inflammatory content, they are also used to automate tasks like scanning web pages so they appear on search engines.

schema.headline: Is Zelensky right to say data centre strikes have taken down Russian bots?

title: The island where locals say data centres are taking their water
description: "Water! Water!" the crowd shouted as it stormed a compound with data centres, armed with empty plastic bottles and jerry cans. There were about 300 of
body: "Water! Water!" the crowd shouted as it stormed a compound with data centres, armed with empty plastic bottles and jerry cans. There were about 300 of them, all residents on the Indonesian island of Batam, and they were furious that the taps at home had run dry, while the data centres in the new Nongsa Digital Park seemed to have enough water to protect their machines from overheating. "Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months... Our water supply had been reliable until the data centres came," Dewi Susanti, one of the protesters, told the BBC. People in her village, Bakau Serip, were now depending on tanker trucks that  dispensed "dirty, cloudy and smelly" water, she said.Batam's water utility told the BBC it was working to improve supply, but did not comment on whether the disruption was linked to demand from the data centres.But BP Batam, the agency overseeing trade and industry, blamed it on a prolonged dry spell and denied allegations from locals that water meant for homes was being channelled to data centres.This is not the first such protest in Batam, whose shrinking reservoirs find themselves under more pressure as the island tries to transform itself into a digital hub.Following protests in August and September, authorities told the firms opening data centres in Batam that they must build their own desalination plants instead of relying on reservoirs for freshwater.  But locals say they are increasingly concerned that they must now compete with servers for water."Reliable data on data centre water use in Indonesia remains scarce, partly because companies treat it as proprietary information," says Agus Hasan, a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology."We should build [data centres] rationally, transparently, and responsibly, and insist on seeing the numbers... [Otherwise] those kept in the dark while their taps run dry will push back, and rightly so," he adds.A backlash has been building against data centres across the world, from the US to the UK to parts of Asia, as tech companies pour billions into AI infrastructure. People are worried about how the huge, windowless buildings might change their neighbourhoods, the constant hum of machines, the security lights that could stay on all night, and the pressure this puts on water and energy resources. While electricity powers the centres, the water keeps the servers from frying – engineers deploy elaborate cooling systems, which consume a lot of water. Research in the US suggests a typical data centre consumes around 300,000 gallons of water a day, or about as much as 1,000 US households. A larger, 50MW facility could take as much water as 2,200 households per day, and enough electricity to power 22,000 homes, according to Malaysia's central bank.It's unclear how much water or electricity the data centres in Batam are consuming. But the island routinely faces water shortages, and the levels are worse this year, possibly because of a historic "super" El Niño. Devoid of natural freshwater sources, Batam's 1.3 million people rely on rainwater collected in six artificial reservoirs. Nongsa reservoir, which supplies water to Bakau Serip, where Dewi lives, would dry up over the next month with no rainfall, simulations by local environmental non-profit group Akar Bhumi Indonesia suggest."The water shortage is affecting our livelihoods... Money that should be used to buy rice is now spent on water drums," Dewi says. "My husband has to wait up overnight to get water, and then go straight to work the next morning."Batam's water utility had earlier said that it would consider measures like cloud seeding should the water shortage continue. When asked about the recent protests, they pointed us to earlier statements.Authorities in Batam have approved 10 data centres, six of which will be located in Nongsa Digital Park. Two are up and running, while a third is under construction. At least six more are currently under review for approval, BP Batam told the BBC.Official figures put investment in data centres on the island at more than $6.7bn (£5.1bn) as of mid-2026, spurred in part by demand from Singapore, which is just an hour away by ferry.Singapore paused construction of data centres in 2019, citing land and energy constraints. It lifted the ban in 2022 after introducing new efficiency standards, which prompted investors to look elsewhere. Singapore has long been promoting the Riau Islands, which includes Batam, and the Malaysian state of Johor as "complementary" regions. Quick to absorb the spillover, Johor approved data centre projects worth tens of billions. But this soon drew the ire of residents frustrated with noise, dust and water shortages. The state has since tried to regulate how much water and electricity data centres consume.Across the strait, Batam is just as attractive to investors – from the US, China, Australia, Singapore – because of relatively low operating costs, proximity to Singapore and connections to major subsea cable routes.Nongsa is home to a 13,000-sq-m data centre by Hong Kong-based private equity firm Gaw Capital and Indonesian developer Sinar Primera. In April, Singapore's DayOne signed a deal with an Indonesian state utility to build one of the country's largest data centres with around 450MW capacity, enough to power 350,000 average households.  In June, DayOne, chip maker Nvidia and Australian AI start-up Firmus Technologies announced a 360MW "AI factory". By 2030, power demand from data centres in Batam is expected to cross 1,100MW, which is enough to power nearly a million homes, according to the official estimates.The BBC has contacted DayOne, Sinar Primera and Gaw Capital for comment.Meanwhile, the spate of construction is worrying locals in Batam who urged authorities to prioritise their needs."Don't just sit at the top and keep approving these projects. Come down here and see for yourselves what we are wrestling with," says Marlinda, who lives in the district of Sei Beduk, which is also facing water shortages. "We want the government to pay attention to ordinary people," another resident told the BBC."Don't make billion-rupiah investments while ordinary people are made to suffer... We are not asking for anything extravagant. We just want our water supply restored."

schema.headline: The island where locals say data centres are taking their water

title: Tata boardroom feud is testing a trusted business empire
description: Before dawn breaks over Mumbai, Mansi Kadam begins preparing vada pav, a savoury snack synonymous with the western Indian city, for the day's customer
body: Before dawn breaks over Mumbai, Mansi Kadam begins preparing vada pav, a savoury snack synonymous with the western Indian city, for the day's customers. One ingredient is non-negotiable: Tata salt.When asked whether she would ever consider switching brands, her reply is a reminder of an old Hindi ad jingle, "If it's salt, it has to be Tata."She knows little about the developments unfolding in the boardroom of the Tata group, one of India's oldest and most influential business empires that makes everything from salt to software.But her instinctive loyalty points to a question confronting the group: Can one of India's most trusted brands remain insulated from a public battle over power, governance and control?A recent public disagreement between the board of Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata group and Tata Trusts, its principal shareholder, has put a spotlight on the conglomerate.At the centre of the dispute are two issues - the proposed public listing of Tata Sons and the reappointment of chairman N Chandrasekaran. Most of the Tata Sons board, including its biggest minority shareholder SP Group, supported the decisions.But Noel Tata, chairman of majority shareholder Tata Trusts, has opposed both resolutions. He maintains that a public listing would dilute the group's philanthropic ethos and is likely to get both decisions overturned at its annual general meeting."When we say this is a governance crisis, it's a misalignment of interests between the board [of Tata Sons] and the shareholders [Tata Trusts]," Shriram Subramanian, head of independent corporate governance firm InGovern Research, told the BBC.While he does not expect the brand's image to be affected immediately, he flags concerns over the leadership's ability to navigate the challenges.Disagreements within the Tata Group have been simmering since the death of former chairman Ratan Tata - Noel Tata's half-brother who designated him successor after his death - in 2024. For many Indians, Ratan Tata's philanthropy and leadership had become inseparable from the brand. His death triggered widespread mourning and experts say it left a leadership void in the group's image with the public.The Tata group has topped India's most valuable brand list by valuation consultancy Brand Finance since 2018, according to the group's website.Tata Sons, the business entity, is described by the group as the "fastener keeping the many disparate elements of the whole together".Tata Trusts, which represents seven philanthropic trusts that own the majority stake in the group, is widely regarded as its moral compass, guiding the businesses on social impact and philanthropy.For many Indians, both the entities together make up what most companies cannot buy - trust.Now with these entities in rival corners, that is coming under strain."Once upon a time, there was a unified audience which said the Tatas are good people with good governance. Today, the opinion is divided," said Harish Bijoor, business and brand strategy consultant.While most consumers appear unfazed, the dispute has polarised other stakeholders including business partners, investors and employees. Some view it as corporate power politics, others as a genuine governance debate, but few agree on which side is right, Bijoor said."This conflict has brought the Tatas into conversations everywhere, which is not good as they have always liked to be out of it," he says.The group has traditionally preferred being low profile about philanthropy and conflict resolution.The Tata group did not respond to BBC's email with detailed questions.Founded by Jamsetji Tata in 1868, the Tata group expanded under JRD Tata who transformed it into a professionally managed conglomerate. Ratan Tata drove its global ambitions through acquisitions.Tata group, which has a combined market value of more than $260bn (£195.6bn) and employs hundreds of thousands of people in more than 100 countries, is not new to controversies.The conglomerate has faced protests over industrial projects, scrutiny of its Indian telecom business during a spectrum allocation controversy, a high-profile dispute with Japan's Docomo and, more recently, questions over Air India's performance.Some of its business decisions have also drawn attention, particularly Tata Steel's troubled Corus acquisition, though other overseas bets such as Tetley and Jaguar Land Rover were successful and helped expand the group's global footprint.Its biggest controversy was in 2016 when the Tata Sons board abruptly removed Cyrus Mistry as chairman and brought back Ratan Tata as interim head. Mistry, heir to the SP Group, was chosen by a team led by Ratan Tata himself. It led to a long battle which ended in 2021 with the Supreme Court ruling in the Tatas' favour. Last month, journalist Sucheta Dalal wrote in her column for Moneylife magazine that the Tata group has "weathered serious governance storms" and enjoys "special privileges available to no other business group [referring to a tax exemption granted to Tata Trusts for holding shares in Tata Sons]" because of a reputation built over decades.Most Tata watchers agree.In an email interview, Morgen Witzel, a fellow at Exeter Centre of Leadership who wrote a book on the brand in 2010, cited several examples on the group's connection with people.At Jamshedpur in Jharkhand state, where the group set up India's first integrated steel plant and an industrial city, it provides healthcare and education to people in hundreds of villages. Watchmaker Titan supports employees who want to leave and start their own businesses. Tata Motors at Pune has supported thousands of female entrepreneurs, he points out."It is the concatenation of all of these things that builds trust because people see that, by and large, Tata is there to serve their needs rather than just take their money," Witzel said.But while the group has weathered other storms, this time, the divide is within.The boardroom tussle has increasingly spilled into the public domain, with Tata Sons and Trusts clashing through legal notices and conflicting statements.Venu Srinivasan, vice-chairman of Tata Trusts and a nominee director on Tata Sons' board, has sought a probe into alleged governance lapses at some trusts. The trusts deny the lapses.Noel Tata has made two proposals to avoid listing the company.First, that the Tata Sons board buy back a portion of SP Group's minority stake as a "fair and equitable solution" to the latter's demand to monetise their stake. Secondly, restructure Tata Sons by merging with itself two businesses which would change the way it is classified by India's central bank,  helping the group potentially avoid a listing.It is not clear whether he can pull this off, given that unlike Rata Tata, he had not consolidated power yet."Ratan Tata's larger-than-life image is, to some extent, the reason behind the current conflict. Everyone was deferential towards him and his successor was known only after his death through his will," says Subramanian.Had Ratan Tata overseen the succession himself, the transition would have been smoother, he says.Brand expert Bijoor calls for the Tata group to put together a "white paper" on how the conflict plays out in the end. "They stood for transparency, and they must never shed that."How the influential group manages these tensions may offer a glimpse into its future. The outcome will be watched closely across corporate India, where Tata's governance and business practices have long been regarded as a benchmark.

schema.headline: Tata boardroom feud is testing a trusted business empire

title: Super El Niño breaks sea temperature record weeks ahead of expected peak
description: Although the most widespread impacts are expected later this year and into 2027, El Niño's influence is already being felt across parts of the world.T
body: Although the most widespread impacts are expected later this year and into 2027, El Niño's influence is already being felt across parts of the world.The strength of an El Niño does not automatically determine the scale of impacts in any one location. Regional effects can vary considerably from one event to another.However, some common patterns are emerging when compared with previous super El Niños.During the 1997-98 event, severe drought across south-east Asia contributed to extensive peat and forest fires, while parts of East Africa experienced devastating floods.The event also helped make 1998 the warmest year on record at the time.A similar pattern developed during the 2015-16 El Niño. Severe drought and wildfire activity returned to parts of south-east Asia, while southern Africa experienced one of its worst droughts in decades, triggering a major humanitarian crisis.Another recurring signal is tropical cyclone activity. Strong El Niño events typically suppress Atlantic hurricanes while boosting activity across parts of the Pacific, a pattern that has also been observed during 2026.The World Meteorological Organisation says drought and flood-related disruption is already being reported in several regions, with growing concerns over food security in parts of East Africa and the Asia-Pacific.Forecasts from both the European Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasts and the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration indicate El Niño is likely to peak in December.Dr Hausfather said the latest projections were "astonishing" and are likely to set new records "by a remarkable amount".

schema.headline: Super El Niño breaks sea temperature record weeks ahead of expected peak
